1 System Overview 
The MT8676 device is a highly integrated and scalable application automotive processor with rich multimedia features and 
AI capabilities. The chip integrates 4 Arm® Makalu and 4 Arm® Klein, along with a powerful multi-standard video codec. 
Furthermore, an extensive set of interfaces is integrated for camera modules, external audio components, UFS/SD cards, 
and external modules. 
 
The ARM® Makalu application processor offers substantial computing power to support the latest open-source operating 
systems, as well as In-Vehicle-Infotainment (IVI) and Cockpit Domain Controller (CDC) applications. The ARM® Klein provide 
adequate computing power for dedicated tasks, such as software-based graphic rendering and real-time operating system 
in critical execution environments. 
 
In addition, the SMMU with unique performance enhancements for hard real-time masters, integrated in MT8676, provide 
a straightforward hardware mechanism that minimizes the virtualization overhead of hypervisors. This is particularly 
beneficial when multiple operating systems coexist for various application domains, thus optimizing overall system 
performance. 
 
The new Gen 7 APU in MT8676 is capable to address the latest AI trends in achieving maximizing effective performance in 
AI-multimedia, AI-camera, and AI-voice experiences. The APU Gen 7 also aims to ensure that AI-enhanced technologies to 
perform sustainably across conditions for extended durations. 
 
The multi-standard video accelerator and an advanced audio subsystem are also integrated to provide advanced 
multimedia applications and services such as streaming audio and video, a multitude of decoders and encoders. 
 
The high-performance CPU, DSP , and hardware coprocessors are combined to provide a powerful modem subsystem 
capable of supporting NR Sub6, LTE Cat 18, Category 24 HSDPA downlink and Category 7 HSUPA uplink data rates, as well 
as Class 12 GPRS, EDGE. 
 
MT8676 also embodies wireless communication devices, including WLAN, Bluetooth and GPS. With four advanced radio 
technologies by Combo chipsets, MT8676 provides the best and most convenient connectivity solution in the industry. 
 
The chip supports rich automotive camera features, such as around view monitoring, back view monitoring, automotive 
driving recoding, and driver monitoring. These features can be employed via the maximum 16x video stream inputs with 
MIPI-CSI2, or Ethernet AVB inputs. The rich display interface (MIPI-DSI and DP) allows for support of up to 6 display panels, 
further enhancing its usability in various automotive applications.

1.2 Platform Features 
• General 
− Cockpit, 2 MCU subsystems architecture 
− Supports UFS boot 
− Supports LPDDR5X 
 
• AP MCU subsystem 
− 4 Arm® Makalu cores with each core having 64 KB 
L1 I-cache, 64 KB L1 D-cache and 512 KB L2 cache 
− 4 Arm Klein cores with each core having 32 KB L1 I-
cache, 32 KB L1 D-cache. And 2 Klein cores shared 
128 KB L2 cache. 
− Shared 4 MB L3 cache 
− NEON multimedia processing engine with 
SIMDv2/VFPv4 ISA support 
− DVFS technology with adaptive operating voltage 
from 0.65V to 1.05V for Makalu core, and from 
0.55V to 1.05V for both Makalu cores and Klein 
cores 
 
• APU for CV and NN 
− Top performance: Fix8: Up to 1.15 TOPS; Fix16: Up 
to 0.28 TOPS; FP16: Up to 0.28 TOPS; FP32: Up to 
0.07 TOPS 
− C, OpenCL and Halide programming language 
− Advanced software framework for automatic filing 
and fusion 
− Enhanced data sharing for CV/NN algorithm 
− Native transcendental function for special 
operations 
− Vector FPU to support high precision requirement 
applications 
− 512 KB local memory (L1 memory) 
 
• APU to support NN applications with high-
performance and high-power efficiency 
− Top performance: 8(A) x 4(W) 20 TOPS, 4(A) x 4(W) 
20 TOPS, 8(A) x 8(W) 20 TOPS, 16(A) x 8(W) 10 
TOPS, 16(A) x 16(W) 5 TOPS FP16/BF16 5 TOPS 
− Supports layer based mixed precision 
− Simultaneous pipelined hardware function block 
(CONV/ACT/POOL/EWE/BILINEAR) 
− Enhancement of layer fusion to further reduce 
DRAM/TCM memory bandwidth 
− Enhancement of non-CONV OP performance 
− Supports Android NN asymmetric quantized data 
format 
− Supports weight decompression to reduce DRAM 
BW 
 
• APU memory subsystem 
− 2nd level data memory: Scenario based allocation 
policy, up to 3 MB 
− eDMA for data movement and data format 
conversion  
 
• MD MCU subsystem 
− High-performance multi-core and multi-thread 
processor architecture 
− High-performance AXI bus interfaces 
− General DMA engine and dedicated DMA channels 
for peripheral data transfer 
− Power management for clock gating control 
 
• MD external interfaces 
− Dual SIM/USIM interface 
− Interface pins with RF and radio-related peripherals 
(antenna tuner, PA, etc.) 
 
• Security

• External memory interface 
− LPDDR5X up to 24 GB (4 channels with 16-bit data

− Memory clock up to LPDDR5X-7500 
− Self-refresh/partial self-refresh mode

− Programmable slew rate for memory controller’s

MHz RF bandwidth per component carrier (CC) and

1.4 Connectivity Features 
MT8676 includes four wireless connectivity functions: 
 
• WLAN 
• Bluetooth 
• GPS 
• FM receiver 
 
The RF parts of those four blocks are placed on chip 
MT6637. With four advanced radio technologies 
integrated on one chip, MT8676 and MT6637 are the 
best and most convenient connectivity solution in the 
industry, implementing advanced and sophisticated radio 
coexistence algorithms and hardware mechanisms. It 
supports dual antenna sharing among 2.4 GHz 
Bluetooth, 2.4 GHz/5 GHz/6 GHz WLAN and 1.575 GHz 
for GPS. The enhanced overall quality is achieved for 
simultaneous voice, data and audio/video transmission 
on mobile phones and media tablets. The small footprint 
with low-power consumption greatly reduces PCB layout 
resource. 
 
• Supports integrated Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/GPS 
− Dual antenna for WLAN 
− Single/Dual antenna for WLAN/GPS/Bluetooth 
− Self-calibration 
− Single TCXO and TMS for GPS, BT and WLAN 
− Best-in-class current consumption performance 
− Intelligent BT/WLAN coexistence scheme that goes 
beyond PTA signaling (e.g., transmit window and 
duration that take into account protocol exchange 
sequence, frequency, etc.) 
 
• Wi-Fi 
− Dual-band (2.4/5/6 GHz) with 2-stream 802.11 
ax/ac/a/b/g/n MAC/BB/RF SoC, 20/40/80/160 MHz 
bandwidth, MCS0~11 (1,024-QAM) 
− 802.11 d/e/h/i/j/k/r/v compliant 
− Security: WFA WPA/WPA2/WPA3 
personal/enterprise, AES-CCMP , WPI-SMS4, GCMP , 
WPS2.0, WAPI (hardware) 
− QoS: WFA WMM, WMM PS 
− 802.11n optional features: STBC, A-MPDU, Blk-Ack, 
RIFS, MCS feedback, 20/40 MHz coexistence (PCO), 
unscheduled PSMP 
− Supports 802.11w protected managed frames 
− Supports 802.11ax STBC Tx/Rx, 4T2R beamformee, 
2T2R beamformer, MU-MIMO Rx, WoWLAN 
− Supports MediaTek proprietary low-power green AP 
mode for portable hotspot operation 
− Auto rate control for optimizing the signal range and 
performance 
− Supports Wi-Fi direct (WFA P2P standard) and Wi-Fi 
display 
− Supports Wi-Fi HotSpot 2.0 
− Integrated PA with 2.4G max. power 23 dBm for 
CCK, and 5G max. power 19 dBm for 54 mbps OFDM 
− 2.4G Rx sensitivity is -76.5 dBm for 11n HT20 MCS7; 
5G Rx sensitivity is -63 dBm for 11ac VHT80 MCS9 
− Supports 32 multicast address filters and 
TCP/UDP/IP checksum offload 
− Per packet Tx power control 
 
• Bluetooth 
− Supports Bluetooth v5.3 core spec. 
− Supports BT/BLE dual mode 
− Integrated PA with 14 dBm (class 1) transmit power 
− Rx sensitivity @chip-in: 
▪ GFSK -97 dBm 
▪ DQPSK -96 dBm 
▪ 8-DPSK -90 dBm 
▪ BLE_1M -100 dBm 
▪ BLE_2M -97 dBm 
▪ BLE_500K -102 dBm (PER < 30.8%) 
▪ BLE_125K -106 dBm (PER < 30.8%) 
− Supports BT/Wi-Fi/LTE/NR coexistence 
− Supports 7 BT links and 16 BLE links 
− Supports packet loss concealment (PLC) function for 
better voice quality 
− Supports wideband speech 
− Supports mSBC and SBC including mono and stereo 
− Supports secure connection with AES128 and 
ECC256 
− Supports adaptive frequency hopping with built-in 
channel assessment method

2.2.3 Storage Condition 
1. Shelf life in sealed bag: 24 months at < 40°C and < 90% relative humidity (RH). 
2. After the bag is opened, devices subjected to infrared reflow, vapor-phase reflow, or equivalent processing must be: 
• mounted within 168 hours in factory condition of 30°C/60% RH, or 
• stored at 20% RH. 
3. Devices should require baking before being mounted if they are placed 
• for 192 hours at 40°C +5°C/-0°C and < 5% RH in low temperature device containers, or 
• for 24 hours at 125°C +5°C/-0°C in high temperature device containers.

3 MCU and Bus Fabric 
3.1 Microcontroller Unit System (MCUSYS) 
3.1.1 Introduction 
The microcontroller unit system (MCUSYS) is a subsystem responsible for running the operating system and application 
programs. It comprises two different types of CPU, including four Cortex-A510 cores and four Cortex-A710 cores, into a 
single cluster (DynamIQ). It also provides different levels of power efficiency and computing power to satisfy a wide range 
of system power and performance requirements. The power efficiency of four little cores (Cortex-A510) is specially 
optimized to minimize the power consumption in daily usage scenarios and lightweight applications. For performance 
driven applications, the combination of powerful three Cortex-A710 and one high-speed Cortex-A710 are capable of 
handling heavy tasks and providing the best user experiences. 
 
The MCUSYS supports DVFS technology which allows the CPU to run at different frequencies and voltage configurations for 
different application requirements. Besides DVFS, the power of each CPU core can be turned off individually when not 
used.  In the standby mode, the MCUSYS can be completely shut down to further save power consumption and optimize 
the battery usage on mobile devices. 
 
3.1.2 Features 
3.1.2.1 Little Cores, Cortex-A510 Specifications 
• 4-core Arm® Cortex-A510 MPCoreTM 
• Supports Armv9 architecture for both 32-bit and 64-bit execution states 
• Armv9 extensions, Armv9 extensions, cryptography extensions, RAS extensions, Armv9 (LDAPR instructions only)  
• Supports scalable vector extension (SVE) and SVE2 SIMD instruction set, offering advanced SIMD and floating-point 
architecture 
• 32 KB L1 I-cache and 64 KB L1 D-cache 
• 128 KB private L2 cache for each CPU 
• DVFS technology with adaptive operating voltage 
 
3.1.2.2 Big Cores, Cortex-A710 Specifications 
• 4-core Arm® Makalu MPCoreTM 
• Arm v9.0 architecture with 64-bit execution states 
• Cryptographic and RAS extensions 
• Supports SVE and SVE2 
• Supports advanced SIMD and floating-point 
• MPAM – Memory system partitioning and monitoring 
• 64 KB L1 I-cache and 64 KB L1 D-cache 
• 512 KB private L2 per core

3.1.2.4 Clock Modes between DynamIQ and AXI Bus Fabric

3.2 On-Chip Memory Controller 
3.2.1 Introduction 
The on-chip memory controller provides the boot ROM (read only memory) and SRAM (static random-access memory) 
resources. 
 
3.2.2 Features 
The memory controller has the following features: 
• 256 KB on-chip ROM, with memory access protection and detection 
• 256 KB on-chip SRAM, with memory access protection and detection 
• Chip ID

3.2.3.1 Boot ROM Power Down Mode 
The “boot ROM power down” mode (also referred as “power down mode”) is used in the following scenarios. 
 
1. After the system boot, the boot ROM is powered down and prevented from any probe of ROM content. 
2. In MCDI (multi-core-deep-idle), it is the bootstrap for the suspend/resume CPU. 
 
The power down mode can be entered by setting SRAMROM_SEC_CTRL.sramrom_sw_rom_pd_reg = 1. The bus interface 
unit returns a far jump instruction when receiving the read transactions. The jump address offset is always zero, so the 
program enters an infinite loop until being reset. 
 
The power down mode can also be entered by discounting specified timing cycles. The amount of timing cycles can be 
specified by setting SRAMROM_BOOT_ADDR register. Once the counter reaches zero, the SRAMROM automatically enters 
the power down mode. 
 
3.2.3.2 Boot ROM FPC Mode 
The “boot ROM FPC (function pattern code)” mode is mainly used in the function pattern mode. When the chip is trapped 
into the FPC mode, the AXI-FPC bridge blocks all the transactions to the ROM address by returning a far jump instruction 
with jump address specified in SRAMROM_FPC_BOOT_ADDR of the default value of 0. The AXI-FPC bridge then 
automatically unblocks the transaction when the FPC program is downloaded to the SRAM memory address space. 
 
3.2.3.3 On-Chip SRAM Security Protection 
The on-chip SRAM can be partitioned into four regions with different security protection configurations. The bus interface 
unit performs the permission check based on the settings, records the first violated address in the SEC_VIO_ADDR 
registers, and issues interrupts to the host processor. The violation interrupt can be cleared by a write to SEC_VIO_ACK.

3.3 External Interrupt Controller (EINTC) 
3.3.1 Introduction 
The external interrupt controller (EINTC) processes all off-chip interrupt sources and forwards interrupt request signals to 
the AP MCU. 
 
3.3.2 Features 
The EINTC supports up to 123 external interrupt signals and performs the following processes to the interrupt signals 
coming from external sources: 
 
• Polarity inversion 
• Edge/Level trigger selection 
• De-bounce with a configurable 32 kHz clock (optional) 
 
According to the register configuration, the external interrupt source is forwarded to the AP MCU built-in interrupt 
controller with different IRQ signals, eint_irq or eint_direct_irq. The EINTC generates wake-up events to the AP MCU.

3.4 System Interrupt Controller (SYS_CIRQ) 
3.4.1 Introduction 
For processors which contain embedded genetic interrupt controllers (GIC) in it, the MCUSYS should keep feeding the clock 
and power to make the interrupt functional. However, reserving an always-on (or frequently turned on) domain in the 
MCUSYS is power ineffective due to power/leakage overhead introduced by a higher clock ratio and deep submicron 
processes. 
 
The system interrupt controller (SYS_CIRQ) is a low power (also a second level) interrupt controller designed to work 
outside the MCUSYS that the MCUSYS can be completely turned off to improve the system power consumption without 
losing interrupts.  
 
3.4.2 Features 
The SYS_CIRQ supports up to 784 interrupts which can configure the following attributes individually. 
 
• Polarity inversion 
• Edge/Level trigger selection 
 
The 784 interrupts feed through the SYS_CIRQ and connect to the GIC in the MCUSYS. When the SYS_CIRQ is enabled, it 
records the edge-sensitive interrupts and generates a pulse signal to the CPU GIC when the flush command is executed.

3.5 Infrastructure System Configuration Module (INFRACFG) 
3.5.1 Introduction 
The infrastructure system configuration module (INFRACFG) provides reset, clock and miscellaneous control signals in the 
infrastructure system. 
 
3.5.2 Features 
The INFRACFG provides the following control signals to the functional blocks inside the infrastructure system: 
 
• Software reset signals 
• Clock gating control signals 
• Dynamic clock management control signals 
• AXI bus fabric control signals 
• Sleep protect control signals 
 
3.5.2.1 DCM in Details 
The dynamic clock management (DCM) function slows down the clock frequency for power saving when the system is in 
the idle state automatically. 
 
The clock frequency in the DCM mode is set to quarter of the original clock. The ratio of clock frequency slow-down is 
controlled by the INFRA_DCMFSEL register. 
 
After the bus idle signal is low, it takes several cycles of latency to make the slow-down clock return to the normal 
frequency. The cycle number varies with the runtime status of the clock gating logic and causes minor performance impact. 
To minimize the impact when the system is in heavy load status, the INFRA_DCMDBC register controls the cycle count once 
the bus idle signal is asserted. Set the debounce cycle to be longer and enable the function to reduce the probability of the 
system entering the DCM mode. 
 
3.5.2.2 AXI Fabric Control 
The AXI fabric control registers prevent the system bus from hanging up caused by improper accesses while some parts of 
the system are in the power-down state. The sleep protector can get the functions above. Refer to the corresponding 
control registers in 3.5.3.

3.6 External Memory Interface (EMI) 
3.6.1 Introduction 
The external memory interface (EMI) controller schedules requests from the masters and issues commands to the DRAM 
controller (DRAMC) in an efficient way. The block conducts flow control for the DRAMC and masters to avoid DRAM stall or 
data overflow/underflow. It also minimizes the latency of processor path to enhance the performance and tries to increase 
the DRAM efficiency. The block also informs clock control to gate the clock for the time when it does not find any 
transaction. This block is designed to supply an EMI clock frequency of 728 MHz that can be scaled down to 660 MHz, 625 
MHz, 466 MHz, 333 MHz, and 200 MHz. 
 
3.6.2 Features 
The EMI controller receives AXI master commands and issues them to the the DRAMC. It supports all AXI transaction type 
commands, except for the fixed and cache commands. There are plenty of schedule options to schedule the command, 
which are: 
 
• Starvation control 
• Bandwidth regulator 
• Latency regulator 
• High priority 
• Page hit control 
• Read/Write turnaround prevent control 
• Memory-protect unit (DRAM and APB) 
 
3.6.3 Block Diagram 
In MT8676, the EMI controller is used as a bridge of several systems and the DRAMC. For cortex APMCU system, or 
multimedia masters (e.g., display, video encoder, video decoder, and camera), or GPU, APU and peripherals, two 128-bit 
AXI ports are provided for the connection. Besides, there are two 128-bit AXI ports for connecting to the modem MCU and 
modem 2G/3G/4G/5G hardware.

3.7.3 Block Diagram 
The major blocks of the DRAM controller are command decoder, command pool, bus scheduler, timing controller DDR PHY 
and response generator. 
 
The requests from the arbiter are pushed to the command pool to wait for execution in order. The bus scheduler inspects 
the precharge/active pool and command FIFO and decides which DRAM bus command, e.g., PRECHARGE, ACTIVE, READ or 
WRITE, is issued to the DRAM bus. The goals of bus scheduler are to raise the bus utilization rate and lower the response 
latency. The timing control unit is responsible for the integrity of the DRAM bus timing such as pre-charge to active delay 
(tRP), active to command delay (tRCD) and bus turnaround time. The bus scheduler refers to the information and chooses 
the next DRAM bus command. The DRAM interface unit is responsible for generating DRAM bus commands, transmitting 
data and DQS to DDR DRAM and receiving data and DQS from the DDR DRAM. The response generator produces the 
response signals for all DRAM agents such as DLE and RDAT.

3.8 Application Processor DMA (AP_DMA) 
3.8.1 Introduction 
The MT8676 application processor DMA (AP_DMA) serves data transfers between the memory and peripherals. 
 
3.8.2 Features 
• Supports up to 29 channels of simultaneous data transfers 
• Compliant with system bus (AXI) 
• Data FIFO of 128 bits embedded in the DMA channel 
• Peripherals and channels: 
– UART x 4 (Tx/Rx channels are separated, 8 channels in total) 
– BTIF x 1 (Tx/Rx channels are separated, 2 channels in total) 
– I2C x 19 (I2C x 7, I3C x 12) 
– Triggers DMA transmission through the handshaking signal from a peripheral 
• Source/destination configuration 
– Only one side (either the source or the destination) is programmable; the other side can be selected as the specified 
peripheral. 
• Burst size/burst length of 8 bytes/1 beat 
• TrustZone 
– The corresponding channel is set as the secure channel, if SEC_EN (AP_DMA_I2Cx_SEC_EN, 
AP_DMA_UARTx_TX_SEC_EN or AP_DMA_UARTx_RX_SEC_EN)[0] = 1 
– If the channel is set to a secure one, it can issue secure requests, and its configuration registers can only be accessed 
via secure masters. 
• Interrupt notification when the FIFO data is over/under a certain threshold. 
• Scheduling scheme 
– Round-Robin (RR): If many channels are triggered simultaneously, the triggering priority will depend on the channel 
number. The channel with a smaller number has a higher priority, e.g., channel 0 > channel 1 > channel 2. 
• Cache coherency not supported

For better bandwidth efficiency, every read request from the Tx DMA to the Tx VFF is 8 bytes. If VFF_VALID_SIZE < 8 bytes, 
the DMA does not issue any read request to the Tx VFF, even if the DMA FIFO is empty. It could be problematic if the total 
data size pushed to the VFF by the CPU is not 8-byte aligned, the last remaining data (< 8 bytes) can be kept in the VFF 
permanently. To resolve this issue, the software should set up the “Tx FLUSH” register to enable the DMA to issue a read 
request to get the last remaining data in the VFF. 
 
 
Figure 3-11. UART Tx VFF data flow diagram 
 
3.8.3.1.2 UART Rx VFF DMA 
In the Rx VFF DMA mode, the data transfer direction is opposite to that in the Tx VFF DMA mode. After the UART pushes 
data to the VFF with handshaking signals, VFF_WPT is then updated by the hardware. On the other hand, VFF_RPT is 
updated by the CPU after CPU pops data from the VFF if VFF_VALID_SIZE > 0. 
 
There is also a threshold (RX_VFF_THRE) to trigger interrupts. If VFF_VALID_SIZE ≥ RX_VFF_THRE, the CPU can pop data 
after receiving IRQ. In other words, if there is a lot of valid data stored in the VFF, the DMA will trigger IRQ which informs 
the CPU to pop data. If the CPU cannot pop data from the VFF immediately, the data from the UART might be lost. To avoid 
this, the DMA can inform the UART through side-band signals, and the CPU will receive IRQ if VFF_LEFT_SIZE ≤ 
RX_FLOW_CTRL_THRE. The software can assert RTS if IRQ is received. 
 
Every write request from the Rx DMA to the VFF is 8 bytes. If the total data from the UART is not 8-byte aligned, the last 
remaining data (< 8 bytes) will be kept in the DMA FIFO permanently. There are two methods to solve this issue: 
 
1. Set up the “Rx FLUSH” register manually, and DMA will issue a write request to pop the remaining data from the DMA 
FIFO to the VFF.

3.9 Command Queue DMA (CQ_DMA) 
3.9.1 Introduction 
The command queue DMA (CQDMA, or CQ_DMA) enables data transfers between different slaves, which there are several 
slaves in a platform, and the major one is external memory (e.g., SDRAM). 
 
3.9.2 Features 
• Supports 4 GDMA channels 
• Compliant with the system bus (AXI) 
– Supports unaligned data transfer (byte alignment) 
• A data FIFO of 16 x 8 bytes embedded in each DMA channel 
• Source/Destination configuration 
– Both source and destination are programmable. 
• Burst size of 8 bytes 
• Burst length of 1 to 7 beats 
• DMA transfer length (maximum and minimum) (unit: byte): 
– Without address-wrapping -> (256M - 1, 1) 
– With address-wrapping -> (512M - 2, 1) 
• Source or destination address fix mode 
• Source or destination address wrapping mode 
• Source and destination address increment mode 
• Fixed pattern mode 
• Bandwidth limiter 
• TrustZone: 
– The corresponding channel is treated as a secure channel if SEC_EN(CQ_DMA_G_DMA_SEC_EN)[0] = 1. 
– If the channel is set to a secure one, it can issue secure requests, and its configuration registers can only be accessed 
via secure masters (interrupt notification). 
– Completion of transfers for a specified amount count 
– Supports the lock mechanism to SEC_EN and DOMAIN in every channel 
– SEC_EN and DOMAIN in every channel in a secure world by default 
– LOCK and DLOCK in every channel in a secure world by default 
• Supports descriptor mode 
 
3.9.3 Block Diagram 
The CQDMA serves for memory copies and registers read/write in batches, and it supports the address wrapping function, 
burst mode transfer, increment and fixed mode on the source/destination address which both addresses are programmed 
as memory space or control register space.

3.9.4.2 Address Wrapping Mode 
This section describes the wrapping mechanism, where WRAP_EN (CQ_DMA+0x0018) [15] is the enable bit of the address 
wrapping function. There are two address wrapping modes that are determined by WRAP_SEL (CQ_DMA+0x0018) [20].

2. Set CQ_DMA_G_DMA_SRC_ADDR (CQ_DMA+0x001C) and CQ_DMA_G_DMA_JUMP_ADDR (CQ_DMA+0x002C) as the 
start address and jump address respectively. 
3. CQ_DMA_G_DMA_DST_ADDR (CQ_DMA+0x0020) is the destination address. 
4. Use CQ_DMA_G_DMA_LEN1 (CQ_DMA+0x0024) and CQ_DMA_G_DMA_LEN2 (CQ_DMA+0x0028) as the transfer 
length. There are two sub-transitions. 
5. Copy CQ_DMA_G_DMA_LEN1 (CQ_DMA+0x0024) size data from CQ_DMA_G_DMA_SRC_ADDR (CQ_DMA+0x001C) to

6. Copy CQ_DMA_G_DMA_LEN2 (CQ_DMA+0x0028) size data from CQ_DMA_G_DMA_JUMP_ADDR (CQ_DMA+0x002C) 
to (CQ_DMA_G_DMA_DST_ADDR (CQ_DMA+0x0020) + CQ_DMA_G_DMA_LEN1 (CQ_DMA+0x0024)) continuously.

3.10 System Companion Processor (SCP) 
3.10.1 Introduction 
The system companion processor (SCP) is a tiny processor subsystem with MDSP RV55NN processor and peripherals. The 
power domain of the sensor hub subsystem is always-on and the clock source is very low power. The special design in the 
power domain and the clock source makes the subsystem suitable to run applications, such as voice wake-up, sensor hub 
and future tasks when the entire SoC is in the suspend mode. The subsystem is connected to the infra-bus and therefore 
can access DRAM, audio system SRAM and the other hardware resources through the infra-bus. The subsystem also has 
another slave interface for the APMCU to configure the subsystem. 
 
3.10.2 Features 
The MDSP RV55NN processor is a 32-bit microprocessor core with the following features: 
• 32 KB I-cache and 32 KB D-cache 
• AXI interface & prefetch 
• 8-stage pipeline 
 
The SCP features: 
• 1 MDSP RV55NN core 
• 2 MB L2TCM 
• An AXI master interface for the SoC site memory access (registers/DRAM) 
• An AXI slave interface for APMCU configuration 
• Inter-processor interrupts to APMCU 
• 6 32-bit down-count timers for RV55NN core, clock source is selectable 
• An interrupt controller for RV55NN core 
• Supports 32-input external interrupt with debounce function 
• 7 I2Cs 
• 4 SPIs 
• 2 UARTs 
• 32-bit GPIO 
• Direct path to the PMIC wrapper 
• Watchdog timer

3.11 System Level Cache/Buffer (SLC/SLB) 
3.11.1 Introduction 
The system level cache (SLC) controller schedules requests from the external memory interface (EMI) and issues 
commands to the DRAM in an efficient way. It also minimizes the latency of processor path to enhance the performance 
and reduce DRAM accessing power.  
 
The system level buffer (SLB) controller schedules requests from the masters and issues commands to the SRAM in an 
efficient way. 
 
The SLC/SLB also informs clock control to gate the clock when it does not find any transaction. The SLC/SLB is designed to 
supply the same clock with the EMI. 
 
3.11.2 Features 
• SLC features 
– 4 MB with 16-way cache 
– 64-byte cache line (block) size 
– Write-through policy 
– Bypass mode with coherency 
▪ Tag access on demand; no data operation 
▪ Reserved way allocation 
– Constrained read/write allocation 
▪ Supports 64-byte-aligned 64B/128B payload (all write strobe bits must be asserted) 
▪ Single outstanding per-ARID 
– MPLRU replacement policy 
– Speculative fetch 
▪ EMI early abort for bandwidth reduction 
 
• SLB features 
– SLC and SLB can be runtime partitioned on the basis of way. 
– SLB can be accessed via CEN_EMI path and dedicated SLB bus. 
– Individual SLB port 
▪ Memory allocated address (0x0f00_0000~0x0f3f+fff) 
▪ Max. 256-bit interface (for 728 MHz, total bandwidth = 23 GB/s x DRAM channel) 
▪ Pipeline latency: 7T 
– Via EMI  
▪ Configurable memory allocated address 
▪ AXI addressing: Access range must not cross 128 bytes boundary 
▪ Pipeline latency: 15T

4.2.5 Programming Guide 
4.2.5.1 TOPRGU Initialization 
Enable the dual-mode reset when the TOPRGU is firstly initialized. Since WDT_MODE cannot be reset and the WDT 
(including WDT_SWRST) IRQ mode is also disabled if system reset is triggered through WDT_SWRST, the registers can only 
be reset by SYSRSTB. 
 
The following registers cannot be reset by the TOPRGU: 
• WDT_MODE 
• WDT_STA 
• WDT_NONRST_REG 
• WDT_NONRST_REG2 
• WDT_REQ_MODE 
• WDT_REQ_IRQ_EN 
 
4.2.5.2 Watchdog Timer 
• Trigger WDT_RESTART right after WDT_LENGTH is updated. 
• WDT_SWRST can be triggered without wdt_en set to 1’b1. 
• Trigger WDT_RESTART before setting wdt_en to 1’b1. 
 
4.2.5.3 IRQ Mode 
Since the dual mode reset is on by default, all reset requests are in the IRQ mode also by default. This means that the 
interrupt is triggered (instead of the system reset) immediately. To trigger the system reset but not the interrupt, change 
the corresponding configuration of each reset request which can be configured as reset or IRQ separately. 
 
4.2.5.4 Dual Mode Reset 
The dual mode reset is the system watchdog reset after the TOPRGU triggers the interrupt. The watchdog timer should be 
enabled to fulfill this function. 
 
In this mode, the watchdog timer is AUTO-RESTART after the interrupt is triggered. The AP should clear WDT_STA after 
receiving the interrupt from the TOPRGU. The watchdog timer is restarted to {WDT_LENGTH, {9{1’b1}}} once the interrupt 
is issued, and the watchdog reset is triggered after the timer expires.

5 Peripherals 
5.1 Peripheral System Configuration Module (PERICFG) 
5.1.1 Introduction 
The peripheral system configuration module (PERICFG) provides reset, clock and miscellaneous control signals in the 
peripheral system and IPs. Each module inside the peripheral system has its own software reset and clock gated control 
(power-down control). The hardware dynamic clock management (DCM) of the peripheral system is also contained. 
 
5.1.2 Features 
The PERICFG provides the following control signals to the functional blocks inside the peripheral system: 
 
• Software reset signals 
• Clock gating control signals 
• DCM control signals 
• AXI bus fabric control signals 
• Sleep protection control signals 
 
5.1.2.1 Dynamic Clock Management (DCM) 
The DCM function slows down the clock frequency for power saving when the system is in the idle state automatically. 
 
The clock frequency in the DCM mode is set to quarter of the original clock. The ratio of the clock frequency slow-down is 
controlled by the PERI_DCMFSEL register. 
 
After the bus idle signal is low, it takes several cycles of latency to make the slow-down clock return to the normal 
frequency. The cycle number varies with the runtime status of the clock gating logic and somehow causes some minor 
performance impacts. To minimize the impacts, when the system is in a heavy load status, the PERI_DCMDBC register 
controls the cycle count once the bus idle signal is asserted. Setting the debounce cycle to be longer and enabling the 
function can reduce the probability of the system entering DCM mode. 
 
5.1.2.2 AXI Fabric Control 
The AXI fabric control registers prevent the system bus from hanging up caused by improper accesses while some parts of 
the system are in the power-down state. The sleep protector can get the functions above. Refer to the corresponding 
control registers in 3.5.3.

5.2 General-Purpose Input/Output (GPIO) Control 
5.2.1 General Descriptions 
The I/O pins can be programmed for multiple purposes, including general-purpose input/output (GPIO), NAND, SPI, etc. By 
setting up the GPIO_MODE register, a specific I/O is selected for a specific function. 
 
 
Figure 5-1. GPIO block diagram 
 
All functions should comply with the priority rule. When there is more than one I/O set as the same output function, all of 
the selected I/Os are able to output specific signals. When there is more than one I/O set as the same input (or bi-
directional) function, only the I/O with the largest GPIO index works functionally.

5.3 Keypad Scanner 
5.3.1 Introduction 
The keypad (KP) supports 3*3 key matrix (9 keys). 
 
5.3.2 Features 
The KP interface includes 3 columns and 3 rows (see the block diagram in the later chapter). The key detection block 
provides the key pressed, key released and debounce mechanisms.

The key detection block senses the change and recognizes whether a key has been pressed or released each time. 
Whenever the key status changes and becomes stable, a KEYPAD IRQ will be issued. Then the MCU can read the key(s) 
pressed directly in the KP_MEM1, KP_MEM2, KP_MEM3, KP_MEM4 and KP_MEM5 registers. The status register can only 
be changed by the key-pressed detection FSM. 
 
5.3.4 Theory of Operations 
KP detects one key, or two keys pressed simultaneously in any combination. Figure 5-3 and Figure 5-4 show the one-key 
pressed condition. Figure 5-5 illustrates the case where two keys are pressed. Since the key-pressed detection depends on 
the HIGH or LOW level of the external keypad interface, if the keys are pressed at the same time and one key exists in the

5.4 Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter  
5.4.1 Introduction 
The universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter (UART) provides full duplex serial communication channels between the 
chip and external devices. The UART has M16C450 and M16550A operation modes, which are compatible with a range of 
standard software drivers. The extensions are designed to be broadly software compatible with 16550A variants, but 
certain areas offer no consensus. 
 
In common with M16550A, the UART supports word lengths from five to eight bits, an optional parity bit and one or two 
stop bits, and this word length is fully programmable by a CPU interface. A 16-bit programmable baud rate generator and 
an 8-bit scratch register are included, along with separate transmission and received FIFOs. Eight modem control lines and 
a diagnostic loop-back mode are provided. The UART also includes two direct memory access (DMA) handshake lines 
which are used to indicate when the FIFOs are ready to transfer data to CPU. Interrupts can be generated from any of the 
several sources. 
 
After hardware reset, the UART is in M16C450 mode. Its FIFOs can be enabled and the UART can enter M16550A mode. 
The UART adds further functionality beyond M16550A mode. Each of the extended functions can be selected individually 
under software control. 
 
5.4.2 Features 
The features of UART are as follows: 
 
• Provides 3 channels of UARTs 
• UART1 is a 4-pin (Tx, Rx, CTS, RTS) UART channel.  
• UART0 and UART2 are 2-pin (Tx, Rx) UART channels. 
• Supports both M16C450 and M16550A operation modes 
• Compatible with standard software drivers 
• Transfer system: Asynchronous  
• Data length: 5 to 8 bits  
• Hardware flow control: CTS/RTS-based automatic transmission and reception of control  
• Software flow control: Uses special character Xon/Xoff to do software flow control 
• Baud rate is programmable from 300 bps to 3 Mbps. 
• Baud rate error: Less than 0.25 % 
• Interrupt request: Receive interrupts/transmit interrupts  
• Data transfer: DMA (transmit/receive) transfer is supported.

5.4.3 Block Diagram 
 
Figure 5-6. Block diagram of UART 
 
Figure 5-6 shows the block diagram of UART. It consists of the first in first out (FIFO), the finite state machine (FSM), APB 
BUS I/F and modem control. Because of full-duplex serial communication, UART has Tx and Rx channels, and each channel 
contains a FSM (Tx FSM & Rx FSM) and a 32-byte FIFO (Tx FIFO & Rx FIFO). The FSM is used to indicate the current transfer 
stage of Tx and Rx channel. The Tx FIFO and Rx FIFO store the data to be sent or the data received from outside. Through 
APB BUS I/F, the system can access the configuration and status registers of UART, read the received data or write the data 
to be sent. UART can support the function of hardware flow control through modem control. The UART signal descriptions 
are included in Table 5-3.

5.4.4 Communication Protocol 
UART communication protocol is as follows: 
 
• 1-bit start bit must be low. 
• The data bit length is 5~8 bits. 
• The parity check can be odd parity or even parity. 
• The stop bit length is 1~2 bit(s). It must be high.

UART Enhancement Features 
The UART provides more powerful enhancements than the industry-standard 16550: 
 
Hardware flow control: Use two dedicated signals, clear to send (CTS) and request to send (RTS) signals, to indicate UART is 
ready to get data or send data. When CTS is low, UART can start to transmit data. As long as CTS is active, UART is not 
allowed to send data. RTS going low means UART FIFO in received circuit is sufficient to receive data. UART is not allowed 
to receive data when RTS is high. This feature is very useful when the interrupt service routine (ISR) latency is hard to 
predict and control in the embedded applications. The MCU is relieved of having to fetch the received data within a fixed 
amount of time. 
 
Software flow control: Use special character Xon/Xoff to do software flow control. Special character Xon/Xoff is software 
programmable. When Xoff is received, UART transmission is halted. The transmission will not be resumed until Xon is 
received. 
 
Notes:  
1. In order to enable any of the enhancements, the enhanced mode bit, EFR[4], must be set. If EFR[4] is not set, IER[7:5], 
FCR[5:4], and MCR[7:6] cannot be written. The enhanced mode bit ensures that the UART is backward compatible 
with software that has been written for 16C450 and 16550A devices. 
2. When the oversampling ratio between UART clock and baud rate is less than 8, it is necessary to enable guard time 
function in your UART Tx device to make MediaTek UART Rx work properly. Otherwise, frame error could happen and 
the received data could get corrupted.

Data Transmission 
If the Tx holding register (THR) is empty (FIFOs are disabled) or Tx FIFO is reduced to its trigger level (FIFOs are enabled), Tx 
holding register empty (THRE) bit of the LSR is “1” and the transmitted data can be written in the THR. 
 
When THR is not empty (FIFOs are disabled) or Tx FIFO is increased to its trigger level (FIFOs are enabled), Tx starts 
transmission automatically. 
 
Software can write transmitted data into THR by asserting transmit interrupt (IIR[5:0] = 000010b) or polling the THRE bit 
status as “1” directly. 
If FIFOs are enabled, the transmitted data can be written into the THR. The data will be transferred to Tx FIFO directly. 
 
Data Reception 
If the Rx buffer is becoming full or a byte is being transferred into Rx FIFO, the DR bit of the LSR is “1” and the received data 
can be read by Rx buffer register (RBR).

5.5 Super Speed Universal Serial Bus (SSUSB) 
5.5.1 Introduction 
The SuperSpeed universal serial bus (SSUSB) provides a USB3.1 port with the USB3.1 Gen1 peripheral role, and the port is 
with the USB2.0 dual role capability. It contains a pair of U3 Gen1 PHY and U3 Gen1 MAC for SuperSpeed connection, and 
a pair of U2 PHY and U2 MAC for high-, full- and low-speed connections. 
 
The USB2.0 dual role capability allows the port to support On-the-Go (OTG) host and the peripheral. For a USB2.0 host 
role, this port is controlled by the eXtensible host controller (xHC) which is used to manage all devices connected through 
its root hub ports. For a peripheral role, the port is controlled by the device (DEV) controller.

5.6.4.2 SPI Master Sampling Time Adjustment 
When the SPI is operating at a high rate, the circuit delay and the EVB delay need to be taken into consideration. Figure 
5-30 gives a general view of how circuit delay and EVB delay influence SPI sampling result.

Figure 5-30. SPI master sampling time 
 
The SPI master generates a SCK_gen inside the SoC. Due to circuit delay, it takes SCK_gen waveform tSCK_dly time to arrive 
at SCK pin. Then, the SPI slave receives the SCK_pin waveform, and puts data on the MISO_pin after tV time. At last, MISO 
data costs tMISO_dly time to reach the SPI master for sampling. If the total delay – tSCK_dly + tV + tMISO_dly + tEVB_dly 
exceeds half the SCK period, the SPI master would sample the wrong MISO data. In this case, GET_TICK_DLY (SPIn Base 
address+0x0018) [25:22] should be set to postpone the SPI sampling time.  
The following formula shows how the appropriate GET_TICK_DLY is calculated: 
 
GET_TICK_DLY * Tclk – ½ TSCK < Ttotal_dly < GET_TICK_DLY * Tclk + ½ TSCK 
 
Note: Tclk is the module clock period. TSCK is the SCK period. Ttotal_dly = tSCK_dly + tV + tMISO_dly + tEVB_dly.

5.6.4.3 SPI Master Bus Busy Status and Transaction Complete Interrupt 
The SPI master provides the busy status of the bus: BUSY (SPIn Base address+0x0020) [0].  
When BUSY (SPIn Base address+0x0020) [0] = 0, an SPI transaction is presently under way. The software must NOT try to 
start a new SPI transaction.  
When BUSY (SPIn Base address+0x0020) [0] = 1, no SPI transaction is ongoing. The software may start a new SPI 
transaction and it could confirm the SPI bus status by polling the bit of spi_busy beforehand. 
When a transaction is completed and interrupt FINISH_IE (SPIn Base address+0x0018) [16] is enabled, the SPI master 
controller sets FINISH (SPIn Base address+0x001C) [0] and asserts an SPI interrupt to notify the software that the SPIM 
transaction is completed.  
If both PAUSE mode PAUSE_EN (SPIn Base address+0x0018) [4] and PAUSE interrupt PAUSE_IE (SPIn Base address+0x0018) 
[17] are enabled, the SPI controller sets PAUSE (SPIn Base address+0x001C) [1] and asserts an SPI interrupt to notify the 
software that the SPIM transaction is completed. At this time, the SPI controller is in PAUSE_IDLE state, and is ready to 
receive the resume command by RESUME (SPIn Base address+0x0018) [1].

5.8 Inter-IC (I2C)/Improved Inter-IC (I3C) Controller 
5.8.1 Introduction 
The inter-IC (I2C)/improved inter-IC (I3C) controller is a two-wire serial interface. The two signals are SCL and SDA. Both SCL 
and SDA are bi-directional data signals that can be driven by either the master or the slave. This generic controller supports 
the master role and conforms to the I2C/I3C specification.  
 
5.8.2 Features 
The features of I2C/I3C controller are as follows: 
 
• I2C compliant master mode operation 
• Adjustable clock speed for LS/FS mode operation 
• Supports 7-bit/10-bit addressing 
• Supports high-speed mode 
• Supports slave clock extension 
• Manual transfer mode 
• Multi-write per transfer 
• Multi-read per transfer 
• Multi-transfer per transaction 
• Combined format transfer with length change capability 
• Active drive/wired-and I/O configuration 
• Start multiple transfer repeatedly 
• Single data rate transfer 
• Dynamic address assignment 
• Common command code 
• Secure slave address 
 
5.8.2.1 Manual Transfer Mode 
The controller supports the manual transfer mode. When the manual mode is selected, in addition to the slave address 
register, the controller has a built-in 8-byte deep FIFO for I2C and a 16-byte deep FIFO for I3C, which allows the MCU to 
prepare bytes of data for a write transfer, or to read bytes of data for a read transfer. 
 
5.8.2.2 Transfer Format Support 
This controller is designed to be as generic as possible in order to support a wide range of devices that might utilize 
different combinations of transfer formats. Figure 5-37 to Figure 5-44 illustrate the transfer format types supported 
through different software configurations.

5.8.2.3 Secure Design 
The MediaTek I2C supports secure I2C/I3C slave and non-secure I2C/I3C slave which share an I2C bus. 
 
APB secured channel 
As mentioned above, the MediaTek I2C allows many drivers to share an I2C bus. These drivers are parking at different APB 
channels which are split by memory map from bit8 to bit11, which means every 4 KB memory map for I2C is split into 16 
sets of 256B. These channels are named from 0 to 15. In the default design, channel 15 is always in the secure domain 
which serves the other 256B security-related settings. For example, users can configure channel 15 and make channel 1 a 
secure channel.

The most important thing for secure design is the secure slave address. The MediaTek I2C/I3C controller supports four sets 
of I2C/I3C slave addresses locked in the secure domain. For example, there is a device used for front camera with face ID, 
and the slave addresses are 0x3 and 0x5; if 0x5 is locked into the secure environment, it is no possible to fetch data from 
slave address 0x5 which serves the face ID. 
 
Signal secured 
For the debugging purpose, the MediaTek I2C/I3C controller supports SCL/SDA snooping, but this feature works if and only 
if the driver gets the bus authority. For example, if there are two drivers, AP and the camera control unit (CCU) sharing an 
I2C bus, when AP is transferring data, both SCL/SDA will always be high for the CCU.  
 
Secured common command code 
The MediaTek I3C supports three ranges and two exact secured common command codes (CCC) which help the mixed 
I2C/I3C bus with the secure slave and the non-secure one set by a central driver. For example, when there is dynamic 
address assignment (DAA) for face ID, which is accessed firstly by the AP driver, the dynamic address (DA) will not be 
modified by hikers. 
 
5.8.2.4 Arbitration Design 
The MediaTek I2C supports secure slave and non-secure slave that shares an I2C bus. This section briefly explains how it 
works. 
 
Round robin 
From APB channel 1 to channel n, the round robin arbitration is adopted. Channel 0 is always executed. For example, in the 
case of channel 3, the design copies all settings including FIFO data to channel 0 first. Then it resets (finite state machine) 
FSM and starts the setting. In arbitration, channel 0 is locked and cannot be configured by software. 
 
Interrupt 
Every channel has its own MCU_INTR mentioned in the register map. This control register marks the MCU to which the 
channel issues an interrupt. For example, if two drivers use channel 1 and channel 2, and MCU_INTR are 0x1 and 0x2 
respectively, the interrupt for channel 1 will send an interrupt to MCU 1 while channel 2’s will be sent to MCU 2. There is a 
conflict: if MCU_INTR sets 0x1 for channel 1 and 0x3 for channel 2, the design cannot recognize that channel 2 issues an 
interrupt to the MCU 1 after channel 1 has issued an interrupt to MCU 1. To solve this conflict, the design in this case will 
hang the arbitration, and wait for software to clear the interrupt issued to the same MCU. 
 
Error handling 
If and only if the interrupt status is larger than 0x1, the arbitration will stop and open the authority for channel 0 until MCU 
interrupted handling error is done. For example, when MCU 1 at channel 2 gets an interrupt status 3, it can then configure 
channel 0 instead of channel 2 to solve the problem from the slave. When the handling is done, MCU 1 configures channel 
0 START mentioned in the register map 0x2 to kick off the arbitration again. 
 
Secure channel 
During the arbitration, all information will be copied to channel 0 including the secure information. For example, MCU 1 at 
channel 2 is a secure channel. In MCU 1’s turn, channel 0 and channel 2 are both secure channels.

5.9 Pulse-Width Modulators 
5.9.1 Introduction 
Three generic pulse width modulators (PWMs) are implemented to generate pulse sequences with programmable 
frequency and duration for LCD backlight, charging or other purposes. Before software enabling PWM, the pulse 
sequences must be prepared in the memory or registers. Then PWM should read the pulse sequences to generate random 
waveform to meet all kinds of applications (see Figure 5-47). 
 
 
Figure 5-47. Generation procedure of PWM 
 
5.9.2 Features 
The features of PWM are as follows: 
• Old mode 
• FIFO mode 
• Periodical memory and random mode 
• 3DLCM mode 
• Breathing Light mode

5.9.4.3 Memory Mode 
  
Figure 5-51. Memory mode 
 
In the periodical mode, all pulse sequences are repeatedly generated by the number of PWM_WAVE_NUM (PWM base 
address + 0x0028)[15:0]. If PWM_WAVE_NUM (PWM base address + 0x0028)[15:0]=0, Hardware infinitely outputs the 
waveform, and the waveform generation can only be stopped by PWM_ENABLE (PWM global base address + 
0x0000)[31:0]. 
If SRCSEL (PWM base address +0x0000)[5]=1, PWM is in the memory mode. The pulse sequence data is put in memory 
with address set by PWM_BUF0_BASE_ADDR (PWM base address + 0x0010)[31:0] & PWM_BUF0_BASE_ADDR2 (PWM 
base address + 0x003C)[3:0], and the length is PWM_BUF0_SIZE (PWM base address + 0x0014)[15:0]. STOP_BITPOS (PWM 
base address + 0x0000)[14:9] is to indicate the stop bit position in the last 32-bit data.

5.9.4.4 Random Mode  
On the other hand, the pulse sequence is stored in dual memory buffers in the random mode. The format of pulse 
sequences stored in the memory is shown in Figure 5-53. The valid bit is used to indicate that the data is ready in the 
respective memory buffer. The PWM generation should clear this bit after all data in that buffer are fetched. The memory 
buffers are set by address PWM_BUF0_BASE_ADDR (PWM base address + 0x0010)[31:0] and PWM_BUF0_SIZE (PWM base 
address + 0x0014)[15:0] for memory 0, and are set by address PWM_BUF1_BASE_ADDR (PWM base address 
+0x0018)[31:0] and PWM_BUF1_SIZE (PWM base address + 0x001C)[15:0] for memory 1. 
 
The program should prepare for the pulse sequence and set the valid bit to 1 in time before all data in other memory 
buffers are fetched. Otherwise, the hardware should issue the UNDERFLOW interrupt to inform that the pulse generation 
should be stopped since there is no valid data. If the UNDERFLOW interrupt is received, software needs to disable the 
PWM to set valid bit again and enable PWM to restart the pulse generation. 
 
 
Figure 5-53. Random mode 
 
Note: Any kind of memory can be used by the PWM (usually SYSRAM) as long as software can read / write the address. 
Software should issue a request, and PWM can locate an un-used memory and get the address, so users need to assign the 
address and length at PWM_BUF0_BASE_ADDR/PWM_BUF0_SIZE and PWM_BUF1_BASE_ADDR)/PWM_BUF1_SIZE. 
 
5.9.4.5 3D_LCM Mode 
These PWM channels are interrelated. One PWM channel can be selected as the base channel. Other PWM channels can 
be selected as the auxiliary channels in the same phase or in the reverse phase. It can be used with old mode and FIFO 
mode.  
 
For example: 
PWM0 acts as the base channel. 
PWM1 is selected as auxiliary channel, which is in the reverse phase compared with the base channel. 
PWM2 is selected as auxiliary channel, and it is in the same phase compared with the base channel.

5.10 General-Purpose Timer (GPT) 
5.10.1 Introduction 
The application processor X general-purpose timer (APXGPT) includes five 32-bit GPTs and one 64-bit GPT. Each GPT 
supports four operation modes: ONE-SHOT, REPEAT, KEEP-GO, and FREERUN. Each GPT can be operated on one of the two 
clock sources, real-time clock (RTC) (32.768 kHz) or system clock (13 MHz).

5.10.4 Theory of Operations 
The read operation value of the GPT6 64-bit timer is separated into two APB reads that each one is of 32-bit width. The 
read of the value works as the lower word being read first and then the higher word. The read operation of lower word will 
freeze the “read value” of the higher word but will not freeze the timer counting. This ensures the separated read 
operation to acquire the correct timer value. 
 
To program and use the GPT, note the following items: 
• The counter value can be read at any time when the clock source is the system clock. 
• The counter value can be read at any time even when the clock source is the RTC. 
• The comparative value can be programmed at any time. When it is rewritten during count operation, the counter would 
be reset to 0 and restart the count.

5.11 Thermal Controller 
5.11.1 Introduction 
On an SoC platform, thermal management is very fundamental so that an SoC can operate within specific temperature 
constraints while achieving computing performance requirements. Operations under an over-temperature condition for a 
long period of time can cause SoC reliability issues. 
 
The thermal management system on the SoC platform includes several thermal sensors embedded in possible hotspots on 
the die and a thermal controller module for periodic measurement for each hotspot. The measurement results are 
readable by software. However, in order to minimize software efforts for monitoring temperatures, the thermal controller 
generates interrupts to a system handler for abnormal conditions. 
 
5.11.2 Features 
The thermal management system includes the following features: 
 
• Supports up to 4 thermal sensors per bank 
• Programmable periodic temperature measurement 
• 2 independent finite state machines (FSM) for temperature monitoring 
• Different types of low pass filters for thermal sensor readings 
 
5.11.3 Block Diagram 
There are three major building blocks for the thermal control subsystem: the sensing device (thermal sensing micro circuit 
unit (TSMCU)), the convertor (low voltage thermal sensing (LVTS) convertor) and the controller (LVTS_CTRL), as shown in 
Figure 5-57.

5.11.5 Theory of Operation 
5.11.5.1 Interrupt Control Flow 
The interrupt conditions of high and low temperature monitor are shown in Figure 5-58 and Figure 5-59. The software can 
determine which temperature sensors to be monitored. Once any of the following three interrupt conditions occurs in any 
of the monitored temperature sensors, interrupts are generated. 
 
• Cold interrupt: asserted when the temperature crosses and falls below the cold threshold. 
• Hot interrupt: asserted when the temperature crosses and rises above the hot threshold. 
• Hot-to-normal interrupt: asserted when the temperature crosses and falls below the hot-to-normal threshold. 
 
The diagram of FSM diagram is shown in Figure 5-60. The states are described as follows. 
 
• COLD_ST: The temperature is lower than the cold threshold. 
• NORMAL_ST: The temperature is within the hot-to-normal threshold and cold threshold.

5.13 Digital Signal Processor (DSP) 
5.13.1 Introduction 
The digital signal processor (DSP) is responsible for running operating system and application programs. It comprises:  
 
• Two-core Cadence HiFi 3 audio engine DSP 
• AXI3 bus interface unit (in-house MediaTek bus) 
• System power management controller (SPMC) control 
 
The HiFi DSP is a three-slot VLIW machine which can execute up to two 32x32-bit MACs, four 24x24-bit, 32x16-bit and 
16x16-bit MACs per cycle. It has an ability to issue two 64-bit loads per cycle, or one load and one store of 32-bit per cycle 
for the parallel loads and stores of the operand and results. The HiFi 3 DSP offers the additional floating-point precision 
support for enhanced audio and voice processing through an optional single precision floating point unit (SP FPU) which 
can perform eight single precision IEEE-754 floating-point MACs per cycle. Since the audio and voice processing at front-
end is made in frequency domain, both the floating-point and fixed-point MAC operations in the HiFi 3 DSP are enhanced 
to operate on complex data types. 
 
5.13.2 Features 
Two-core Cadence HiFi 3 DSP operates at 800 MHz (0P75V)/26 MHz (0P55V), including:  
 
• 64 KB L1 I-cache 
• 128 KB L1 D-cache 
• 36 KB ITCM 
• 32 KB DTCM 
• Data retention is not supported by pre-fetch buffer, I-cache, D-cache, ITag, or DTag. 
• Joint Test Action Group (JTAG)  
• Universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter (UART) 
• 26 interrupts 
• Supports SPM to control the power sequence 
 
Other features: 
• UART for audio data transmission with Bluetooth 
 
5.13.2.1 Pipeline Stages 
The DSP has a 7-stage pipeline which contains a two-cycle latency for both the instruction-memory fetch and the data-
memory fetch. 
 
• Pipeline length     7 
• Instruction memory fetch latency   2

The DSP host processor includes a cache controller with 64 KB instruction cache and 128 KB data cache implemented to

Write-back is supported on the data cache to improve the cache performance. The data cache can be programmatically

the capability of disabling and re-enabling cache ways in both instruction cache and data cache independently to facilitate 
the power saving. New and modified instructions enable users to clean cache ways before disabling them and initialize 
cache ways when enabling them. When a cache way is disabled, the cache memory block from service is removed, and 
therefore total cache capacity will be reduced by 1/(number of ways in service).

The M-PHY is a high-bandwidth and power-efficient physical layer, with a low-pin count serial interface. It consists of the

The UniPro is the middle layer between the application layer and physical layer, defining data format, flow control, error 
handling and power state management. 
The UFSHCI provides a uniform interface method of accessing the UFS hardware capabilities, so that a standard/common 
driver can be provided for the host controller. In order to support cryptographic operations, a secure engine is included in 
the UFSHCI. 
 
The UFS host controller uses the M-PHY serial interface to connect with the UFS device. 
The interface between the M-PHY and the UniPro is called the reference M-PHY module interface (RMMI). 
The data interface between the UniPro and the UFSHCI is called the Cport interface. 
The control interface between the UniPro and the UFSHCI is called the device management entity (DME) interface. The 
UFSHCI uses the AXI bus protocol to connect to the system bus and for the CPU to visit the host controller.

• PCIe configuration interface to give the bridge layer access to the PCIe configuration space 
• PCIe misc. interface to allow the bridge layer to manage low-power, interrupts, etc. 
 
5.15.3.2 Bridge Layer  
The bridge layer consists of: 
• Internal registers of the PCIe controller 
• Address translator modules to convert between the AXI and PCIe interfaces  
• When transferring PCIe receive requests to the AXI master, the address translator adds the corresponding AXI base 
address and forwards the request to the desired AXI master interface. 
• The address translation method is similar when transferring AXI receive requests to the PCIe interface. 
• An interconnect module to interconnect and arbitrate between input and output flow 
 
5.15.3.3 AXI Layer  
The AXI layer consists of the following three parts: 
• An AXI master interface, which manages requests and completions from bridge layer to AXI 
• An AXI slave interface, which manages requests and completions from AXI to bridge layer  
• An AHB or APB slave interface for bridge configuration

• PERST# asserted and de-asserted: It can be reached by writing 1’b1 to bit 3 of the PCIE_SW register (PCIE_MAC Base 
address + 0x0148). PERST# deasserts at least 100 ms (TPVPERL) after the clock and power are stable. Then, clear bit 3

• Reset PCIe itself: The power-on reset (POR) is the active-low reset used to clear all PCIe controller registers and sticky 
registers. 
• Reset PCIe itself via software control: It can be achieved by setting 3’b111 to bit 2:0 of the PCIE_SW register (PCIE_MAC 
Base address + 0x0148). Wait for an appropriate amount of time, for example, 100 ms, and then clear them to finish 
software reset sequence. 
• Reset secondary bus: It can be reached by writing 1’b1 to bit 22 of PCIE_CONF_HDR15_TYPE1 register (PCIE_MAC Base 
address + 0x103C), which triggers a hot reset on the corresponding PCIe port. Hot reset uses bit 0 (hot reset) in the 
training control field within the TS1 ordered sets. Wait for a minimum reset duration (at least 1 ms) defined in PCI local 
bus specification and then clear bit 26 back to 1’b0 to complete secondary bus reset sequence. 
  
5.15.6 Memory Transactions 
Memory transactions are memory space read and write requests, MRd and MWr TLPs, which are generated and sent over 
the PCIe link, and the respective completion TLPs received in return. 
Features supported by master memory requester include: 
• Maximum memory read request: 128 to 256 bytes, depending on hardware configuration 
• Maximum memory write request: 128 to 256 bytes, depending on hardware configuration 
• 32-bit or 64-bit addressing 
 
For initiating memory read or write requests, memory space enable should be asserted by writing 1’b1 to bit 1 of the 
PCIE_CONF_HDR1 register. Then, you can initiate memory access based on memory-mapped address. The related TLP 
should be passed to target PCIe component based on address-routing rule. 
 
5.15.7 I/O Transactions 
I/O transactions are I/O space read and write requests, IORd and IOWr TLPs, which are generated and sent over the PCIe 
link, and the respective completion TLPs received in return. 
 
Features supported by master I/O requester include: 
• Maximum I/O read request: 4 bytes 
• Maximum I/O write request: 4 bytes 
• 32-bit addressing 
 
For initiating I/O read or write requests, I/O space enable should be asserted by writing 1’b1 to bit 0 of the 
PCIE_CONF_HDR1 register (PCIE_MAC Base address + 0x1004). Then, you can initiate I/O access based on I/O-mapped 
address. The related TLP should be passed to target PCIe component based on address-routing rule.

5.15.8 Configuration Transactions 
Configuration transactions are configuration space read and write requests, CfgRd0, CfgWr0, CfgRd1 and CfgWr1 TLPs, 
generated and sent over the PCIe link, and the respective completion TLPs received in return. 
 
Features supported by master configuration requester include: 
• Maximum configuration read request: 4 bytes 
• Maximum configuration write request: 4 bytes 
• Extended register number: 4 KB extended PCIe configuration header space 
 
For initiating configuration read or write request to target endpoint, specify the bus number, device number and function 
number of corresponding endpoint to the PCIE_CFGNUM register (PCIE_MAC Base address + 0x0140). Then, you can 
trigger the desired configuration request by directly accessing memory from (PCIE_MAC Base address + 0x1000) to 
(PCIE_MAC Base address + 0x1FFF). The related TLP should be passed to target PCIe component based on ID-routing rule. 
 
5.15.9 Message Transactions 
Message transactions use message space to support all prior sideband signals, such as interrupts and power-management 
requests. They are used to support in-band communication of events between devices. 
 
The following groups of messages are NOT supported: 
• Locked transaction 
• OBFF (optimized buffer flush/fill) messages 
 
The following groups of messages are supported: 
• INTx interrupt signaling 
• Power management 
• Error signaling 
• Slot power limit support 
• Vendor-defined messages 
• LTR messages 
 
5.15.10 Interrupt Handling 
5.15.10.1 Interrupt to Local CPU 
If one of the following events occurs, the source of the interrupt is reported in bits 31 to 0 of the ISTATUS_LOCAL 
(PCIE_MAC Base address + 0x0184) register . The host processor can mask or enable each interrupt source independently 
by setting or clearing the corresponding bit in the IMASK_LOCAL (PCIE_MAC Base address + 0x0180) register. 
 
PCIe can issue interrupts to the local processor for the following events: 
• Bit [31]: System error signaled.

5.15.11 Error Handling Function 
PCIe supports hardware-controlled autonomous error reporting and handling to improve fault isolation and recovery 
solution. The following description defines these functions. 
 
• Error recovery: The data link layer handles error recovery. It is based on 32-bit CRC (cyclic redundancy check) error 
detection, TLP sequence number, replay buffer and ACK/NAK DLLP exchange. 
• Replay buffer: The replay buffer, located in the data link layer, stores a copy of a transmitted TLP until the transmitted 
packet is acknowledged by the receiving side of the link. 
• Completion timeout: PCIe controller uses a design-specific timeout mechanism for failed read request transaction in 
order to report error messages and to free completion resources.

5.15.13 PCIe Physical Layer Overview 
5.15.13.1 Overview 
The PCIe PHY (physical layer) handles low-level PCIe protocol and signaling, including data serialization and de-serialization, 
8b/10b encoding/decoding, 128b/130b encoding/decoding (8 GT/s), analog buffers, elastic buffers and receiver detection. 
The primary focus of this block is to shift the clock domain of the data from the PCIe rate to one that is compatible with the 
general logic. 
 
5.15.13.2 Features 
• Standard PHY interface enables multiple IP sources for PCIe logical layer and provides a target interface for PCIe PHY 
vendors 
• Utilizes 16-bit parallel interface for Gen 1 and Gen 2 
• Utilizes 32-bit parallel interface for Gen 3 
• Allows integration of high-speed components into a single functional block  
• Supports direct disparity control for use in transmitting compliance pattern(s) 
• Data and clock recovery from serial stream on the PCIe bus 
• Holding registers to stage transmit and receive data 
• 8b/10b encoding/decoding and error indication 
• 128b/130b encoding/decoding and error indication 
• Receiver detection 
• Selectable Tx margining, Tx de-emphasis and signal swing values 
• Electrical sub-blocks that support 2.5, 5.0 and 8.0 GT/s operation compliant with PCIe Gen 3 electrical specification 
 
5.15.13.3 Block Diagram 
Figure 5-67 shows PCIe PHY block diagram. There are 2 main sub-modules. One is PHYA block, including Tx driver, serializer, 
Rx front-end, CDR and de-serializer. The other is PHYD block, including 8b/10b encoder and decoder, 128b/130b 
encoder/decoder (8 GT/s), and elastic buffers.

6.1.1 Introduction  
The display controller contains the multimedia layer pipeline and the display pipeline. The multimedia layer pipeline is the

sub-pixel rendering, over-drive and demura.

• Supports hardware wide-color-gamut 
• Supports gamma correction and panel rounded corner 
• Supports panel overdrive

6.3 Camera Serial Interface (CSI) 
6.3.1 Introduction 
The camera serial interface (CSI) is based on the MIPI Alliance specification CSI2 v2.1. It supports high-speed serial data 
transfer between the host processor and peripheral devices such as camera modules. According to the data type, the data 
transferred from physical layer can be sent by different virtual channels of image signal processor (ISP) and transmitted via 
this high-speed serial interface. The physical layer (CD-PHY) is configurable to meet different throughput requirements of 
camera modules. 
 
6.3.2 Features 
The CSI engine has the following features: 
 Compliant with electrical characteristics of C-PHY Revision 2.0 
 Compliant with electrical characteristics of D-PHY Revision 2.1 
 Supports throughput up to 6 Gsps per C-PHY trio. (CSI PHY & MAC only, actual data rate reference to ISP speed) 
 Supports throughput up to 6.5 Gbps per D-PHY data lane. (CSI PHY & MAC only, actual data rate reference to ISP speed) 
 Support one 4-data lane D-PHY sensor or 2-lane + 1-lane D-PHY sensor 
 Support one 3-trio C-PHY sensor or 2-trio + 1-trio CPHY sensor 
 Compliant with MIPI CSI2 v2.1 
 Supports CSI-2 long and short packet decoding 
 Supports pixel format of RAW8/RAW10/RAW12/RAW14/RAW16/yuv420 10 bits/yuv422 10 bits/RGB565 
 Escape mode is not supported. 
 Alternate low-power mode (ALP) is not supported.

6.5 Display Serial Interface (DSI) 
6.5.1 Introduction  
The display serial interface (DSI) is a MIPI CD-PHY combo IP, based on MIPI Alliance Specification, supporting high-speed 
serial data transfer between the host processor and peripheral devices such as display modules. The DSI supports both 
video mode and command mode data transfer defined in MIPI spec, and it also provides bi-directional transmission with 
low-power mode to receive messages from the peripheral. The DSI should work with the MIPI_TX_Config module to obtain 
its engine clock from analog macro, and it should work with DMA engines in the previous stage of DISP path to read frame 
pixels from the memory. 
 
6.5.2 Features  
The DSI engine has the following features for the DSI: 
 
• MIPI DSI D-PHY interface (4-lane/1-port) 
‒ Throughput up to 2.5 Gbps for 1 data lane at the highest voltage 
‒ Bi-directional data transmission in low-power mode in data lane 0 
‒ Uni-directional data transmission in high-speed mode in data lane 0~3 
‒ Supports non-continuous high-speed transmission in both clock and data lanes 
‒ Supports DSI-2 for D-option version 2.1 
‒ Supports D-PHY version 1.1 
‒ 2 DSI ports 
• MIPI DSI-CPHY interface (3-trio/1-port) 
‒ Up to 3 trios; each trio is composed of 3 wires. 
‒ Throughput up to 2.187 Gsps for 1 trio at the highest voltage 
‒ Low-power mode is identical as D-PHY mode 
‒ Supports continuous high-speed transmission in all lanes. 
‒ Supports DSI-2 for C-option version 2.1 
‒ Supports C-PHY version 1.0 
‒ Two DSI ports 
• 128-enrty command queue for command transmission 
• Supports 3 types of video mode: sync-event, sync-pulse, and burst mode 
• Pixel format of RGB565/RGB666/loosely RGB666/RGB888/RGB101010/sub-pixel/compression stream 
• Supports command mode frame transmission freerun 
• Supports peripheral TE and external TE signal detection 
• Supports limited high-speed residual packet transmission during video mode blanking period 
• Supports ultra-low power mode control 
• Supports low frame rate (LFR) technique

The video decoder (VDEC) which supports multi-standard video compression formats, is capable of greatly reducing the 
CPU load and achieving high performance video decompression. 
 
The video standards supported by the VDEC include:

 VP9 decoder 4K2K@60 fps/120 Mbps, 8/10 bits

 H.264 decoder: Main/High profile 4K2K@60 fps/160 Mbps, 8 bits 
 H.264 decoder: High 10 profile 4K2K@60 fps/160 Mbps, 10 bits 
 MPEG-4 SP/ASP decoder: 1,080p@60 fps/60 Mbps, 8 bits 
 HEIF decoder: Maximum resolution 16,383 x 16,383 (grid mode up to 20,656 x 15,496 for 320M pixels capture), 8/10 
bits

6.6.3 Theory of Operation 
The VDEC hardware architecture is shown in Figure 6-4. Firstly, the VDEC parses bitstream with entropy decoding; and 
secondly, inverse scan, inverse quant and inverse transformation are used to generate residual samples. The decoding 
pictures use intra/inter prediction to generate prediction sample, depending on the prediction block type. Thirdly, the 
reconstruction module adds the residual samples and prediction samples. Lastly, the deblocking filter filters the boundary 
distortion of the reconstruction samples and sends the result to the DRAM.

The MT8676 VENC is configured by software through the APB interface. As the register is configured, the sequencer sends 
the corresponding control signals to trigger submodules. DMA acquires and stores back the image data and bitstream from 
and to the memory based on the configured address. ME conducts motion estimation to decide the motion vector for later 
encoding. MC conducts motion compensation to give predicted pixel values. TQ conducts the transformation and 
quantization operations, and writes reconstructed pixels to DB and quantized transformed coefficient to EC. DB conducts 
the de-blocking operation and allows DMA to store back the processed frame as the reference for the next frame. EC 
conducts entropy encoding, and the coding can be variable-length code, context-based arithmetic code, or context-based 
variable-length code. The encoded bitstream will be written to the memory by DMA.
